chunks.citation: Malik, OA et al. (2015). A global indicator of wastewater treatment to inform the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). ENVIRON SCI POLICY.
chunks.text: Wastewater is typically collected through sewage pipes in municipal areas. Treatment of wastewater entails a step-wise process that occurs in primary, secondary, and tertiary stages. Primary treatment involves basic screening and filtration processes to remove suspended solid waste and reduce its biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which is an indicator to monitor water quality that assesses the amount of oxygen microorganisms must consume to break down the organic material present in wastewater (US EPA, 2012) . Primary treatment can reduce BOD by up to 30% (Flo ¨rke, 2013) . Secondary treatment uses biological processes to break down the dissolved organic matter remaining after primary treatment. Secondary treatment can remove up to 90% of BOD and total suspended solids (US EPA, 2004) . Any additional step in wastewater treatment is considered tertiary treatment (or ''advanced treatment''), which includes any purification process that continues beyond the previous steps and may require more complex technology such as ion exchange and reverse osmosis to further remove contaminants or phosphorous and nitrogen (World Bank, 2013b; US EPA, 2004) .

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.citation: Badawi, AK et al. (2022). Advanced wastewater treatment process using algal photo-bioreactor associated with dissolved-air flotation system: A pilot-scale demonstration. J WATER PROCESS ENG.
chunks.text: Within the framework of this study, an algal photo-bioreactor combined with a dissolved air flotation system (DAF) was used for the removal of COD, BOD 5 , TSS, TN and TP from primary treated wastewater. The optimum operating conditions for the algal photo-bioreactor were determined through batch experiments, which are pH 7, temperature 25 • C, light intensity 90 μmol m − 2 S − 1 and mixing rate 100 rpm. Those optimal conditions were used in a scaled-up pilot plant treatment system to treat primary treated wastewater from ZENIN WWTP-Egypt. The operation has shown significant results where COD, BOD 5 , TSS, TN and TP have been removal with efficiencies of 56.4%, 61%, 59.2%, 48.3% and 51.7% respectively. These findings have been compared with previous studies. These findings proved the efficacy of algal-bacterial integrated treatment systems combined with DAF as a wastewater treatment technology that does not require any additional tertiary treatment to release the effluent to sewer systems.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: However, these processes are costly, require high energy consumption and generally produce secondary waste which cannot remove the pollutants completely and then puts more pressure on the environment (Ghafari et al., 2008; Kapoor and Viraraghavan, 1997) . In contrast, biological treatment is generally regarded as a better choice for nitrate removal from wastewater due to its advantages of complete contaminants removal, economical and energy-saving. Currently, the complete denitrification process is widely applied for nitrate-containing wastewater treatment (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) . However, the traditional complete denitrification process (Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 )) still presents some shortcomings, including high operational costs due to external organic carbon source requirements (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) , large amounts of sludge yields and inevitable greenhouse gas emission, etc. (Du et al., 2016b) . Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

Wastewater samples were then exposed to UV fluences between 10 and 60 mJ/cm 2 . Following treatment, samples were enumerated for E. coli and total coliforms. Pre-and post-UV exposure samples collected at the wastewater treatment facility were also enumerated as controls. All samples were collected as singlets per event and processed under subdued red light to reduce the effects of photo-reactivation.

chunks.text: The system of hydraulically connected WRRFs presented in this study is modeled after the interconnected system of wastewater conveyance and treatment facilities known as the Joint Outfall System (JOS), which is managed and maintained by the Los Angeles County Sanitation District (LACSD). The JOS provides wastewater treatment services for 4.8 million residents in 73 cities. Designed to take advantage of the regional topography, the JOS conveys the collected wastewater to 7 satellite and 1 centralized WRRF mainly by gravity (See Fig. 1 ). The satellite facilities provide the dual purpose of hydraulically relieving the downstream centralized system and of supplying an alternative water resource to the local communities. Each of the satellite WRRFs can be categorized as an extraction type because the wastewater is directly mined out of the sewer system. The harvested wastewater is subsequently treated to title 22 standards via a treatment train comprising primary sedimentation, activated sludge treatment, coagulation, filtration, chlorination, and de-chlorination. The residual solids produced on-site are discharged in the main trunk sewers of the JOS from which they are transported downstream and treated at the centralized wastewater treatment facility.

chunks.text: The main objective of primary treatment of wastewater is the removal of settleable organic and inorganic solids by sedimentation and skimming. Here, about 50 to 60% of the total suspended solids (SS), and 65% of the oil and grease are removed along with some organic nitrogen, phosphorous, and heavy metals attached to the solids. However, the colloidal particles and dissolved constituents are not removed in this stage. Generally, gravity separation is employed in this step to separate the biosolids using either coagulation, flocculation, flotation or filtration techniques as seen in Fig. 2 . chunks.text: A mass of 300 kg of screenings was sampled from the municipal wastewater treatment plant of Bourg-en-Bresse (Region Rhône-   Alpes, France). The waste was made of a mix of screenings from 15-mm and 3-mm screens and was compacted in the plant. The sample was taken to the laboratory where it was homogenized and divided into 20 sub-samples of 8 kg. The procedure allowed to guarantee a good reproducibility of the sub-samples composition, which was verified analytically. The samples were stored at À18 °C. A digestate sampled from a municipal solid waste (MSW) digester was used as an inoculum, in order to have active microflora and to make easier the start-up of anaerobic process. chunks.text: The target full-scale industrial WWTP was located in Shanghai, China, with a designed daily influent capacity of 40,000 m 3 d − 1 , using a typical A/O treatment process. It was responsible for the treatment of wastewater from a wide variety of companies in an industrial park, as well as a negligible amount of domestic wastewater produced in the park (Fig. 1 ). The received industrial wastewater was divided into five parallel process lines, denoted as Lines A to E, each being equipped with its own equalization, anoxic, aeration and secondary sedimentation tank. The effluent from secondary sedimentation tank was then compiled into four dissolved air flotation tanks, and further treated by a V-form filter, an ozone-contact tank and a biofilter consecutively, before discharge into the sea. As shown in Fig. 1 , the equalization and anoxic tanks of Lines A to C were covered together as Duct 1, the whole secondary treatments of Line D plus the aeration tank of Line C were covered by Duct 2, while the secondary treatments of Line E itself were covered in Duct 3.
